title: Residual connections
summary: Plain networks of 56 layers trained worse than networks of 20: the deeper ones were harder to optimise, not overfitting. A residual connection adds a block's input to its output, y = x + F(x), so the layers only learn the change F (the residual) and can pass x straight through by outputting zero. Because addition passes gradients through unchanged, ∂y/∂x = 1 + ∂F/∂x and the shortcut carries the learning signal back to every block. When shapes differ, the shortcut uses a small projection such as a 1×1 convolution.
llm_link: Every transformer block reads the token vectors, computes an update with attention or a feed-forward network, and adds it back. The vectors flow along one path, the residual stream, with each block writing its contribution into it; without it, models dozens of blocks deep would be very hard to train.
key_ideas: Degradation: deeper plain networks had higher training error, so the problem was optimisation, not overfitting (He et al., 2015).
Residual block: y = x + F(x). The layers learn only the change; F = 0 gives the identity.
Gradient: ∂y/∂x = 1 + ∂F/∂x, so the shortcut carries the signal back intact even when ∂F/∂x is tiny.
x and F(x) must have the same shape; otherwise project the shortcut (e.g. a 1×1 convolution with stride 2).
Transformers: every block adds its update into the residual stream.

quiz.q: Predict the result: a residual block's layers output exactly zero for every input. What does the block output?
quiz.explain: y = x + F(x) = x + 0 = x: the block passes its input straight through.

quiz.q: For y = x + F(x), what is ∂y/∂x?
quiz.explain: Addition passes the gradient through unchanged, so the shortcut contributes 1 on top of the layers' own derivative.

quiz.q: A 56-layer plain network has higher TRAINING error than a 20-layer one. What does that tell you?
options: It is harder to optimise, since a deeper network could in principle copy the shallower one
quiz.explain: Overfitting would show low training error and high validation error. Worse training error points to optimisation.

quiz.q: A block halves the image size and doubles the channels. How do we still add the shortcut?
options: Project the shortcut, e.g. with a 1×1 convolution of stride 2, so the shapes match
quiz.explain: x and F(x) must have the same shape to be added; a small projection makes them match.

quiz.q: What is the residual stream in a transformer?
options: The single path of token vectors that every attention and feed-forward block reads from and adds its update to
quiz.explain: Each block writes its contribution into the same stream, which is why deep stacks remain trainable.

problems.title: Why the shortcut keeps gradients alive
problems.prompt:
Backprop through a chain multiplies local derivatives. Write two functions for a list derivs of each block's local derivative dF/dx:

  • plain_grad(derivs): blocks compute y = F(x), so the gradient reaching the input is the product of all derivs.
  • residual_grad(derivs): blocks compute y = x + F(x), so each block contributes 1 + d; return the product of those.

Use plain loops (no NumPy).
problems.starter:
def plain_grad(derivs):
    g = 1.0
    # TODO: multiply by each d
    return g

def residual_grad(derivs):
    g = 1.0
    # TODO: multiply by (1 + d) for each d
    return g

tests.name: 50 blocks with tiny derivatives
tests.code:
d = [0.1] * 50
assert plain_grad(d) < 1e-40, f'0.1 multiplied 50 times vanishes, got {plain_grad(d)}'
assert residual_grad(d) > 1, f'each residual block contributes 1.1, so the signal survives; got {residual_grad(d)}'

tests.name: layers that output nothing
tests.code:
assert plain_grad([0.0, 0.3, 0.7]) == 0.0, 'one dead layer kills the plain gradient'
assert abs(residual_grad([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) - 1.0) < 1e-12, 'with F = 0 every residual block is the identity, gradient 1'

hints:
for d in derivs:
    g *= d

for d in derivs:
    g *= 1 + d

problems.title: A residual block in NumPy
problems.prompt:
Vectors here are 1-D arrays.

  • residual_block(x, W1, W2): return x + W2 @ relu(W1 @ x), where relu(z) = np.maximum(z, 0). W1 is (h, d) and W2 is (d, h), so the output has x's shape.
  • residual_proj(x, W1, W2, P): when F changes the size (W2 is (d_out, h)), project the shortcut: return P @ x + W2 @ relu(W1 @ x) with P of shape (d_out, d).

tests.name: zero layers give the identity
tests.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.0, -2.0, 3.0])
y = residual_block(x, np.zeros((5, 3)), np.zeros((3, 5)))
assert np.allclose(y, x), f'with W2 = 0, F(x) = 0 and the block must return x; got {y}'

tests.name: adds the update
tests.code:
import numpy as np
r = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = r.normal(size=4); W1 = r.normal(size=(6, 4)); W2 = r.normal(size=(4, 6))
y = residual_block(x, W1, W2)
assert np.allclose(y, x + W2 @ np.maximum(W1 @ x, 0)), 'expected x + W2 @ relu(W1 @ x)'

tests.name: projection when shapes differ
tests.code:
import numpy as np
r = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = r.normal(size=3); W1 = r.normal(size=(4, 3)); W2 = r.normal(size=(5, 4)); P = r.normal(size=(5, 3))
y = residual_proj(x, W1, W2, P)
assert y.shape == (5,), f'output should have the new size 5, got {y.shape}'
assert np.allclose(y, P @ x + W2 @ np.maximum(W1 @ x, 0)), 'expected P @ x + W2 @ relu(W1 @ x)'

hints: return P @ x + W2 @ relu(W1 @ x)
